c.tagline: Powder-white sand, turquoise water, and a sunset over Willy's Rock

card: Widely accepted at hotels, resorts, dive shops and larger restaurants; small beachfront eateries, sari-sari stores, tricycles and market stalls are cash-only — keep PHP on hand for daily spending.

taxi.fare: ₱25-50 shared per person along the main road; ₱150-300 chartered
taxi.fareNote: Boracay banned private cars and vans on the main road in 2018 — official blue/white e-trikes and tricycles are the only motorized transport on the island itself; agree on price before boarding if unmetered.

emergency.police: 911 (national emergency line) or Boracay Police Station (Station 2): (036) 288-3061
emergency.medical: 911 or Boracay Community Hospital / Ciriaco B. Tirol Memorial District Hospital in Kalibo for serious cases
emergency.note: Serious trauma cases are typically airlifted or ferried to Kalibo or Iloilo City; Department of Tourism hotline is 1-386 (domestic) for tourist assistance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: White Beach's beachfront path and Station 2's D'Mall are extremely walkable and barefoot-friendly; the island is long and narrow (~7km) so tricycles or e-trikes are used for cross-island trips, especially in midday heat.

safety.safety: Generally very safe for solo travelers, including women
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare; petty theft (unattended bags/phones on the beach, occasional overcharging by unlicensed tricycles) is the main risk — use officially marked tricycles and secure valuables.

hood_landmark.Diniwid Beach: Hidden cove cliffside footpath from Station 1

avoid.reason: Watch belongings on White Beach at night and around Station 2 bars, and agree water-sports and boat prices firmly up front to avoid overcharging.

hood_desc: Boracay's most scenic and upscale stretch of White Beach, home to Willy's Rock grotto, wide soft sand and higher-end resorts, with a quieter, more relaxed vibe than Station 2.

The bustling heart of the island, anchored by D'Mall's maze of restaurants, bars, souvenir shops and travel agencies; loud, crowded and walkable, with the widest range of budgets and the liveliest nightlife strip.
The narrower, quieter southern end of White Beach popular with backpackers and budget travelers, with fewer crowds and a more local, laid-back feel.

The island's east-coast windward beach, the Philippines' top kitesurfing and windsurfing spot thanks to steady onshore winds; rockier and not swimmable at low tide but full of watersports schools and chill beach bars.

A small, secluded cove just north of Station 1 reached by a cliffside footpath, known for calmer water, a rustic laid-back crowd, and some of the island's best sunset viewing away from the main strip.

water.note: Drink bottled or refill-station water only.

transit.sys: E-trikes and tricycles on the single main road; pump boats (bangkas) for inter-island and mainland transfers
transit.hours: E-trikes run roughly 5am-midnight; jetty boats to Caticlan operate about 5am-8pm regularly, with limited service later
transit.pay: Cash (PHP) paid directly to the driver or boatman; agree on fare before boarding for unmetered chartered trips
transit.map: No formal transit map — the island has one main beachfront path (White Beach) and one inland concrete road (Boracay Main Road) running its length
transit.note: Private cars and vans have been banned from the main road since a 2018 island rehabilitation closure; only permitted e-trikes, tricycles and bicycles operate on-island.

transport.air: Fly into Godofredo P. Ramos Airport (Caticlan, code MPH), a 10-min tricycle ride plus 15-min boat from the island; Kalibo International Airport (KLO) is a further ~1.5-2 hr van/bus ride to Caticlan and serves more international carriers.
transport.train: No rail service anywhere on Panay island; nearest rail options are in Manila.
transport.bus: Overnight buses (e.g. Ceres Bus Lines) run from Manila to Caticlan (~12-14 hrs) via the Nabas/RORO ferry route, then a short boat crossing to Boracay.
transport.ferry: Frequent pump boats cross the Tabon Strait between Caticlan Jetty Port and Boracay's Cagban or Tambisaan jetty in 10-15 minutes, roughly every 30-60 minutes.
transport.car: No private car rentals are usable on Boracay itself; visitors drive/rent only for reaching Caticlan or Kalibo on Panay island, then leave the vehicle before the boat crossing.

airport.name: Godofredo P. Ramos Airport (Caticlan)
airport.distance: ~2km from Boracay Island: 10-min tricycle to Caticlan Jetty Port + 15-min boat crossing + short tricycle to your hotel
airport.transport: ₱500-700 DIY door-to-door via tricycle+terminal fee+environmental fee+boat+tricycle; ₱950-1,050 for a pre-booked private transfer; alt airport Kalibo (KLO), ~1.5-2 hr drive to Caticlan Jetty Port

net.m: Good 4G/5G coverage across the island from Globe and Smart; speeds can slow during peak season crowds
net.w: Free wifi is common in hotels, resorts and cafes but can be slow/unreliable — many travelers rely on mobile data instead
net.gb: Prepaid tourist SIM with ~5-8GB data runs about ₱500-800 (~$8-13)
net.fwn: Networks are usually named after the establishment (e.g. hotel/resort wifi), password given at check-in or on menus
net.ap: SIM cards sold at both airports and at kiosks/malls along D'Mall in Station 2

tip.s: Not obligatory but appreciated — round up or leave ₱50-100 for hotel staff, boatmen and tour guides for good service
tip.r: A 10% service charge is often already added to the bill at resorts/restaurants; if not, 10% is a welcome tip for good service

food.name: Chori burger
food.desc: Boracay's own street snack: smoky grilled Filipino chorizo squashed into a soft bun with tangy sauce and pickled slaw. Best eaten walking the beach.

places.name: White Beach beachfront grills
places.note: Cluster of grill stalls on the beach path where the chori burger became a Boracay institution.

places.name: D'Mall food strip
places.note: Several stalls in and around D'Mall grill them to order until late evening.

places.name: D'Talipapa market stalls
places.note: Cheaper, more local version alongside the wet-market grill counters.

food.name: Paluto seafood
food.desc: Pick live crab, prawns, lapu-lapu or squid at the wet market, then hand it to a nearby kitchen to grill, steam or butter-garlic it for a small fee.

places.name: D'Talipapa Talipapa Market
places.note: The classic cook-your-own-catch market; haggle at the stalls, then eat at the paluto eateries behind.

places.name: Smoke Resto
places.note: Long-running cheap Filipino kitchen doing grilled fish and seafood dishes at local prices.

places.name: Cha Cha's Beach Cafe
places.note: Beachfront kitchen at Boracay Beach Club known for fresh seafood and tropical desserts.

food.name: Chicken inasal
food.desc: Visayan grilled chicken marinated in calamansi, vinegar and annatto, basted with achuete oil and eaten with garlic rice and chicken-oil dip.

places.name: Mang Inasal
places.note: Reliable Ilonggo-style inasal with unlimited rice; the easy budget option on the island.

places.name: Smoke Resto
places.note: Backpacker favourite for grilled chicken and Filipino rice plates around the clock.

places.name: D'Talipapa grill stalls
places.note: Charcoal grills next to the market do inasal and pork barbecue skewers.

food.name: Tapsilog and silog breakfasts
food.desc: Cured beef tapa (or longganisa, or spam) with garlic fried rice and a runny fried egg. The Filipino all-day breakfast plate.

places.name: Jasper's Tapsilog
places.note: Island go-to for tapsilog and its silog cousins, open early for post-sunrise-walk hunger.

places.name: Smoke Resto
places.note: Serves silogs alongside its Filipino menu at some of the lowest prices on Boracay.

places.name: Local carinderias off the main road
places.note: Where island staff eat; silogs and rice meals for well under tourist prices.

food.name: Calamansi muffin
food.desc: Boracay's most-copied souvenir bake: a moist muffin sharpened with native calamansi lime, best warm from the oven with local coffee.

places.name: Real Coffee and Tea Cafe
places.note: Homegrown cafe open since 1996 and the original home of the island's calamansi muffin.

places.name: Cha Cha's Beach Cafe
places.note: Beachfront spot known for house bakes including coconut mango tres leches.

places.name: D'Mall bakeries
places.note: Several stalls sell boxed calamansi muffins as takeaway pasalubong.

food.name: Halo-halo
food.desc: Shaved ice layered with sweet beans, jelly, leche flan and ube, topped with evaporated milk and ice cream. Mix it all before eating.

places.name: Halo Mango
places.note: Island favourite for mango ice cups and halo-halo right off the beach path.

places.name: Jonah's Fruit Shake and Snack Bar
places.note: Nineties-era institution near Willy's Rock doing halo-halo and shakes side by side.

places.name: Mang Inasal
places.note: Dependable, cheap halo-halo with the usual full complement of toppings.

food.name: Mango and calamansi fruit shakes
food.desc: Blended fresh Philippine mango, banana or calamansi with ice; the island's default non-alcoholic drink in the afternoon heat.

places.name: Jonah's Fruit Shake and Snack Bar
places.note: Serving its banana-choco-peanut and mango shakes to Boracay visitors since the 1990s.

places.name: Halo Mango
places.note: Mango-forward shakes and ice cups made with ripe local fruit.

places.name: Real Coffee and Tea Cafe
places.note: Calamansi juice and iced teas to go with the muffins.

food.name: Sunset rum cocktails
food.desc: Local Tanduay rum in buckets, mojitos and calamansi coolers, drunk on the sand as the sun drops behind White Beach.

places.name: Cocomangas Shooter Bar
places.note: Long-established Boracay nightlife landmark famous for its shooter challenge.

places.name: Beachfront bars along White Beach
places.note: Rows of beach bars run happy hours timed to sunset with fire-dancing later.

places.name: Cha Cha's Beach Cafe
places.note: Quieter cocktail spot on the sand with tropical drinks and sunset views.

landmarks: White Beach
Four kilometers of flour-soft white sand and swaying palms facing calm turquoise water make this the Philippines' most famous beach and Boracay's glorious centerpiece.
Willy's Rock
A tidal volcanic outcrop crowned by a statue of the Virgin Mary, this is White Beach's most photographed landmark, best at low-tide sunset.
Puka Shell Beach
Boracay's quieter northern strand is strewn with the crushed puka shells that once made it famous, backed by cliffs instead of crowds.
Mount Luho
The island's highest point, reached by stairs or buggy, delivers a sweeping panorama over Bulabog Bay, reef-laced waters and the whole slender island.
Bulabog Beach
Trade winds transform this east-coast lagoon into one of Asia's premier kiteboarding and windsurfing arenas from November through April.
D'Mall
The open-air maze of shops, souvenir stalls, cafes and calamansi-muffin bakeries at Station 2 is Boracay's buzzing commercial and social crossroads.
Crystal Cove Island
A short banca ride away, this private island park hides two swim-through coves, coral gardens and rustic clifftop viewpoints over the Sulu Sea.
Ariel's Point
Boracay's famous cliff-diving day trip near Buruanga offers leaps from ledges up to 15 meters, plus snorkeling, kayaking and boat-side barbecues.
Diniwid Beach
A rock-framed cove just beyond White Beach's northern tip, reached by a cliffside path, beloved for boutique hideaways and mellow sunsets.
Ilig-Iligan Beach
On the island's untamed northeast, jungle-backed sands, tidal caves and offshore snorkeling around Crocodile Island reward travelers escaping the main strip.

train.note: There is no railway on Boracay or Panay island. The Philippines' only passenger rail is around Manila. Arrive by flying into Caticlan or Kalibo airports and continuing by boat.

bus.note: No international coaches - the Philippines has no land border. Southwest Tours and Ceres buses run the two-hour transfer from Kalibo airport to Caticlan jetty, usually sold as a package with the boat and the terminal fees. On the island itself, e-trikes are the only transport along the main road.

intl.to: Caticlan, Panay (Philippines) - pump boat across the strait, ~15 min
intl.op: Caticlan Jetty Port operators — tickets at the jetty terminal

ferry.note: Boracay is reached only by boat - the pump boats from Caticlan take about 15 minutes and run through the day, with a terminal fee and environmental fee paid at the jetty. Crossings stop when a typhoon signal is raised or the sea is rough, which happens regularly from June to November, so leave a buffer before a flight home. Larger ferries connect Caticlan with Batangas and Mindoro for those travelling overland from Manila.

half.name: Nabaoy River
half.blurb: Clear freshwater river on Panay Island near Caticlan, popular for tubing and traditional kawa hot-bath soaking in giant cauldrons.

half.name: Hacienda Maria
half.blurb: Eco-park in the Buruanga hills with a series of waterfalls and cold spring pools, reached by boat and short hike.
